source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Stockwell_2024_CohortBiasLowVolumeMA.pdf, printed pp. 441-452 (all pages, text layer; Tables 1-3 and Figures 1-2 checked on rendered pp. 445-448). The online supplement (Tables A1-A2, Figures A1-A2 and B1-B5, including the forest plots that would identify the subgroup studies) was not read.

claims.overstatement: Understates one estimate. '25 to 44 g a day ... close to no difference' does not fit the younger-cohort estimate 1.17 (0.98 to 1.40): the point estimate is 17% higher, the interval reaches 40% higher, and without the between-study adjustment the same category was significantly higher, 1.30 (1.05 to 1.60). 'Not statistically clear' would be accurate. '7 cohorts' should be '7 studies' (Table 2 counts studies; the 25 to under 45 g estimate rests on 6). No amount is worded as advice, but the threshold framing can read as a limit; the authors' own caveat that their categories are too broad to locate where risk rises (pp. 449-450) is not in the claim and would guard against that reading.
claims.note: All Stockwell 2024 numbers in the statement and magnitude match Table 2, adjusted column: 45 g/day or more 1.51 (1.25-1.82), 25 to under 45 g 1.17 (0.98-1.40), former drinkers 1.32 (1.13-1.54). The reference group (strictly defined lifetime abstainers, 'people who had never drunk') is named correctly. 'Adjusted' in Tables 2-3 means further adjusted for between-study variation (random study effect), not for confounders; the claim does not call these estimates adjusted, which is right. The subgroup also required follow-up beyond age 55 (to at least 56), which the claim omits (minor). 'Higher death rates from about 45 g a day' reads a category boundary, not an estimated threshold, and it holds only in the younger, strictly referenced subgroup: in the 18 older cohorts with both abstainer biases the 45 g or more point in Figure 2 is about 1.03 with an interval spanning 1 (figure only, no values printed). No participant or death counts are given for any subgroup. Conversions recomputed: 45 g/day = 315 g/week, 25 g/day = 175 g/week, 100 g/week = 14.3 g/day (same).

anchors.locator: Table 2, Adjusted column (studies with median cohort age 55 or younger at recruitment, followed beyond 55, and neither former nor occasional drinkers in the reference; lifetime abstainers = 1.00)
anchors.extracted: 45 g/day or more: 7 studies, 16 estimates, RR 1.51 (95% CI 1.25-1.82), p = .0001. 25 to under 45 g/day: 6 studies, 13 estimates, 1.17 (0.98-1.40), p = .0866. Former-drinker group: 7 studies, 20 estimates, 1.32 (1.13-1.54), p = .0006. 1.30 to under 25 g/day: 6/38, 0.98 (0.87-1.11). All people who drank 1.23 (0.95-1.58); current drinking 1.08 (0.95-1.25). Footnote: 'adjusted' = further adjusted for between-study variation.

Without the between-study adjustment (log-RR analysis only): 25 to under 45 g/day 1.30 (1.05-1.60), p = .0167, significant; 45 g/day or more 1.60 (1.32-1.94); 1.30 to under 25 g 1.10 (0.97-1.24); all people who drank 1.32 (1.06-1.63); current drinking 1.24 (1.12-1.37). Whether death rates are higher from 25 or from 45 g a day depends on the model.

anchors.locator: Figure 2 (RRs adjusted for between-study variation; 6 higher- vs 18 lower-quality studies; values read from the figure)
anchors.extracted: In the 18 studies of older cohorts with both abstainer biases the curve is about 0.84 at 1.30-24 g/day, about 0.89 at 25-44 g/day and about 1.03 at 45 g/day or more, the last with an interval of roughly 0.95 to 1.11 (no values printed). In the younger, strictly referenced studies the points are 0.98, 1.17 and 1.51 (caption says 6 studies; Table 2 has 7 at 45 g or more).

anchors.locator: Discussion, last paragraph before Conclusions (limitations; begins p. 448)
anchors.extracted: The authors state that their lower, medium and higher intake categories are too broad to locate the drinking levels at which mortality becomes significantly higher; that many included studies measured intake over the past week or only 2-3 days, adding uncertainty to who drinks and how much; and, citing the Canadian guidance report, that all-cause mortality cohorts are too prone to bias and confounding to underpin low-risk guidelines.

claims.overstatement: None from this source; the claim is more cautious than the authors, who read their results as a false appearance of benefit created by biased reference groups (p. 448; Conclusions p. 450) rather than as insufficient evidence. Minor: '6 cohorts' and '18 older cohorts' are 6 and 18 studies (Table 3 counts studies; some contribute several cohorts), and the younger-cohort criterion also required follow-up beyond age 55. No amount reads as advice.
claims.note: Every Stockwell 2024 figure in the statement and magnitude matches Table 3 (adjusted = with random study effect; partially adjusted = without): all 107 studies 0.86 (0.83-0.88), 99 studies and 306 estimates; 6 studies 0.98 (0.87-1.11), without the random effect 1.10 (0.97-1.24); 5 studies also with a 30-day intake measure 1.04 (0.95-1.15); 18 older studies with both abstainer biases 0.84 (0.79-0.89); one criterion only 0.88 (0.84-0.92; 51 studies) and 0.88 (0.81-0.95; 18 studies). 107 studies, 4,838,825 participants and 425,564 deaths match the abstract; these totals are for all 107, and no participant or death counts are printed for the 99 with low-volume estimates or for any subgroup. Reference groups named correctly: each study's abstainers; strictly defined lifetime abstainers in the 6-study subgroup; abstainers including former and occasional drinkers in the 18. 'Most studies' included former or occasional drinkers among abstainers: 81 of 99 in Table 1 (82%; editors' arithmetic). Editors' arithmetic recomputed: 0.87 to 1.11 is 13% lower to 11% higher (same); 0.98 against 0.84 gives a ratio of 1.17 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.34), z = 2.23, p = .026 (same; independence is reasonable, the two subgroups being disjoint by cohort age). The printed article does not name the 6 studies (forest plots in online Figures B1-B4, not read). One 10-g drink a week is 1.43 g a day, slightly above the source's 1.30 g cut-off (9.1 g a week), and 25 g a day is 2.5 such drinks; the claim's 'about' covers both. Zhao et al.'s adjusted 0.93 appears here only second-hand, without its interval (p. 446). The search ended 31 July 2021 (p. 442); the 1981 start is not from this source.

anchors.locator: Table 3 (1.3 to under 25 g/day against each study's 'abstainers'), both columns
anchors.extracted: All 107 studies: 99 studies/306 estimates, partially adjusted 0.85 (0.82-0.88), adjusted 0.86 (0.83-0.88). Lower quality: cohort age 56 or more 44/104, 0.84 (0.81-0.87); two abstainer biases 46/121, 0.85 (0.81-0.89); age 56 or more plus both biases 18/33, 0.81 (0.75-0.88) and 0.84 (0.79-0.89); plus poor intake measure 15/23, 0.83 (0.77-0.90). Higher quality: age 55 or less 51/169, 0.88 (0.84-0.92); no abstainer bias 18/78, 0.88 (0.81-0.95); age 55 or less plus no bias 6/38, 1.10 (0.97-1.24) and 0.98 (0.87-1.11), p = .7203; plus good 30-day measure 5/34, 1.14 (1.00-1.29) and 1.04 (0.95-1.15).

107 cohort studies with 724 estimates, 4,838,825 participants and 425,564 deaths; low volume defined as from one drink a week (above 1.30 g/day) to two a day (below 25 g/day); younger cohorts with former and occasional drinkers separated from abstainers RR 0.98 (0.87-1.11); studies meeting neither criterion 0.84 (0.79-0.89).

anchors.locator: Table 1, rows Abstainer biases, World region and other study characteristics (unadjusted mean RRs)
anchors.extracted: Of 99 studies with low-volume estimates, abstainers included both former and occasional drinkers in 46, former only in 27, occasional only in 8, neither in 18. Low-volume mean RR 0.82 (0.76-0.88) with both biases vs 0.99 (0.92-1.06) with neither (p = .0004). Regions: North and Central America 40, Europe and Australia 48, Asia 12 studies. Other one-at-a-time contrasts: median age 19-55 0.93 vs 56-78 0.83; poor-health exclusion 0.97 vs none 0.84; 30-day intake measure 0.99 vs 0.86.

anchors.locator: Method > Overview and Search strategy for relevant studies, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: The 107 studies are the pool of Zhao et al. (2023): 87 identified by Stockwell et al. (2016) plus 20 added; English-language articles published to 31 July 2021, PubMed and Web of Science plus reference lists; same research group (Stockwell, Zhao, Naimi).

The paper answers a critique of Zhao et al. (2023) by the International Scientific Forum on Alcohol Research (described by the authors as having significant alcohol-industry ties) that studies not meeting the pre-registered quality criteria should have been excluded rather than adjusted for.

Studies meeting only one of the two main criteria still showed significantly lower risk (0.88 in both); the authors note that neither criterion alone removes the selection biases, the 55-year cut-off is high, abstainer bias is fully corrected only if former drinkers are moved into the drinking groups, and more higher-quality studies are needed.

anchors.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 444); Table 1, smoking and socio-economic status rows (p. 445)
anchors.extracted: Exploratory, one characteristic at a time and unadjusted: 6 studies with results for non-smokers only gave a low-volume RR of 1.16 (0.91-1.41) vs 0.93 (0.71-1.16) in 7 for smokers only (p = .18); studies controlling for smoking or socio-economic status had lower RRs (0.86 vs 1.01; 0.85 vs 0.97). The authors call these analyses only indicative (p. 447).

key_findings.correction: The curve of the 18 lower-quality studies does not stay close to 1 throughout: it dips to 0.84 at low volume (printed in Table 3 for the same 18 studies: 0.84, 0.79 to 0.89; the figure point is about 0.83-0.84), is about 0.89 at 25-44 g/day and reaches about 1.03 (about 0.95 to 1.11) only at 45 g/day or more. Read: 'stays at or below about 1'. The conclusion that even the highest category was not clearly above these studies' abstainer groups stands.

reporting_issues.note: Also Figure 2's caption (p. 448) says 6 higher-quality studies, though its 45 g or more point (1.51) comes from 7 (Table 2).
Confirmed on the rendered p. 445: e.g. 0.89 (0.74-1.04) and 1.16 (0.91-1.41) are symmetric on the untransformed scale; Tables 2-3 are symmetric on the log scale (e.g. 0.98, 0.87-1.11).
Editors' calculation recomputed: ratio 1.167 (1.019 to 1.336), z = 2.23, p = .026.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2, critically low: items 4, 7 and 15 (critical) are 'no' on what the article shows, so the overall rating does not depend on the provisional items 2, 5 and 8. One domain difference: on item 11 I would rate 'no' rather than 'yes', because the article does not say whether adjusted or crude primary estimates were pooled (it converts crude rates to relative risks and pools them with hazard ratios), which AMSTAR 2 asks of non-randomized studies; no effect on the overall rating.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the abstract and Conclusions state the nonsmoker result (6 studies, unadjusted, one category) as a finding, and the Discussion attributes the between-subgroup difference to selection bias creating a false appearance of benefit (p. 448), from a comparison between groups of studies. The main estimate itself is reported with its interval.

missed: Reporting issue: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 444) lists 'assessed alcohol use over less than 30 days' among the study characteristics with significantly higher low-volume relative risks, but Table 1 (p. 445) gives the higher RR to studies with an intake measure covering at least 30 days (0.99, 0.92-1.05, vs 0.86, 0.82-0.90; p = .0026), and the Discussion (p. 447) lists measures of less than 30 days among the characteristics going with lower risk. The text contradicts the table; the table and Discussion agree, so the Results sentence is the error.

For the threshold claim: Table 2's partially adjusted column (p. 447) makes the 25 to under 45 g category significantly elevated in the younger, strictly referenced studies (1.30, 1.05-1.60), so 'higher death rates from about 45 g a day' depends on the random-effect model; the card records the number (key finding 4) but not this consequence.
